endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Applicable state or specialty regulation requires explicit consent for the use case (e.g., certain genomic or behavioral health applications).

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: NIST further states that addressing, documenting, disclosing, and managing AI risks and potential negative impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.

endorsements.title: Navigating Glioblastoma Diagnosis and Care: Transformative Pathway of Artificial Intelligence in Integrative Oncology
endorsements.quote: Taking informed consent from patients is vital, as they deserve to understand how AI influences their medical care and outcomes.

endorsements.title: Ethical framework for responsible foundational models in medical imaging
endorsements.quote: Establish robust patient consent protocols and maintain high standards of data encryption and privacy measures to ensure compliance with healthcare regulations.

endorsements.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
endorsements.quote: This involves updating consent forms, patient information leaflets, and staff training materials to reflect the presence and role of AI in clinical workflows.

endorsements.title: A six-level clinical autonomy framework for artificial intelligence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: Informed consent processes must therefore evolve, ensuring that patients understand not only that AI is involved, but also the level of autonomy it exercises, particularly the distinction between advisory and executional systems.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring formal consent for higher-risk AI uses changes patient understanding, trust, or outcomes compared with passive notice, and no study documents how often such uses proceed on notice alone. Six sources endorse the practice, one as a framework requirement tied to existing state or specialty consent rules and five as commentary or guidance.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The six endorsements consist of one framework, one guidance document, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not raise certainty, so no effect estimate exists for consent versus notice on any patient or system outcome.

The CHAI playbook ties explicit consent to cases where state or specialty regulation already requires it, such as certain genomic or behavioral health uses. A commentary on the EU AI Act describes updating consent forms and patient leaflets to reflect AI. These sources suggest that some consent duties may already apply, though no source maps which ones.

No study measured the time, staff effort, or workflow changes needed to classify AI uses into the five triggering categories and obtain consent. One dental commentary proposes that consent explain the level of autonomy an AI tool exercises, which would require health systems to document that attribute for each tool before the process could run.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare formal consent with passive notice for AI uses meeting the five criteria, measuring patient comprehension, opt-out rates, trust, staff burden, and whether consent processes identify uses that should not proceed. Baseline audits of how often higher-risk AI uses currently run on notice alone would establish whether the hazard occurs at meaningful frequency.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Consent processes that rely on written forms may perform differently for patients with limited literacy or English proficiency, and health systems adopting this practice would be doing so without data on comprehension in those groups.
